props.title: Harry and Tonto
props.initialSlug: Elderly man and cat road trip across America

sections.content: Harry and Tonto (1974) revolutionized the American road movie by centering it around a 72-year-old protagonist, marking a decisive shift from youth-focused counterculture films like Easy Rider (1969). Art Carney's Oscar-winning performance as Harry Coombes created a template for complex elderly characters that influenced later works like About Schmidt (2002) and The Straight Story (1999). The film's genius lies in how it transforms forced displacement - Harry's eviction from his New York apartment - into a journey of late-life discovery.

sections.content: Director Paul Mazursky captured a pivotal moment in American culture, as traditional urban neighborhoods dissolved and families scattered across the country. The film's cross-country journey structure allowed exploration of 1970s American life through Harry's encounters with hippies, Native Americans, and his own geographically dispersed children. This influenced later films about elderly discovery like The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel (2011) and The Leisure Seeker (2017).

The relationship between Harry and his cat Tonto provides a masterclass in how to use animal companions cinematically without sentimentality. This dynamic influenced later films like Inside Llewyn Davis (2013) and A Street Cat Named Bob (2016), where animals serve as both emotional anchors and mirrors for their human companions' journeys. sections.content: Harry and Tonto helped establish a new genre of films centered on late-life awakening, proving that stories about elderly protagonists could be commercially viable and critically acclaimed. This paved the way for films like Driving Miss Daisy (1989) and Cocoon (1985), which similarly refused to treat their elderly characters as mere comic relief or objects of pity. The film's influence can be seen in contemporary works like The Father (2020) and Nomadland (2020), which continue to explore aging with nuance and dignity.
